Nothing is written to disk until you call `save_model`.
An empty model validates and runs, and answers nothing: the first problems appear with the first block.
Use it to inspect, modify or run an existing model, including the bundled examples once they have been copied into the root.

The log needs a case id, an activity and a timestamp per row (CSV), or XES traces; lifecycle (schedule/start/complete) and resource columns make the draft better.
It is a first draft: read `assumptions` (what the log could not tell, such as shifts or the wait before a case's first activity) and `dropped` before trusting its numbers.
The file must be under the workspace root; a log over a size ceiling, or an XES file with a DOCTYPE, is refused outright, and there is no argument that changes either.
The two lists are cut to fit one reply; the totals say how many there are, and the open model has them all.

Use it to find out what you can `open_model` and which handles `get_model_summary` and `run_model` accept.
This is the tool to call before editing an existing model, and after a batch of edits to check the shape is what you intended.
It is deliberately much smaller than `get_model_json`; reach for that only when you need every field.
Each link is "source -> target"; the ORDER of a block's outgoing links is its branch order (branch 0 first).
Use it only when `get_model_summary` is not enough -- a full layout is large.
It is also what you would hand to another tool that speaks the model file format (see the `naga://reference/schema` resource).
Every tool that changes a model pushes exactly one undo entry, so one `undo` reverses one tool call.
Use it to back out an edit whose returned problems show it was wrong.

Only available while nothing new has been edited since the undo: any fresh mutation clears the redo stack, exactly like the editor.
The normal way to build a model: add CREATE, the processing blocks, and DISPOSE, then `connect` them.
Position is cosmetic -- call `auto_layout` once at the end instead of placing blocks by hand.
A wrong param name or type comes back in "introduced" with code E_PARAM_UNKNOWN / E_PARAM_TYPE and a hint listing the params this type takes.
`params` MERGES rather than replaces, so you can set one value without restating the rest.
Renaming rewires every link automatically.
Unknown names are ignored rather than refused, so removing an already-gone block is not an error.
Expect new problems if you cut the flow in half -- the answer says which.
Links are ORDERED: the n-th link you add out of a DECIDE is its branch n, matching `probs[n]` / `conditions[n]`.
Add branches in the order you want them, or fix the order afterwards with `reorder_branches`.
Only DECIDE and LOGIC may have more than one outgoing link.
A branching block may send TWO branches to the same target (a DECIDE where two cases end the same way): the second call returns `index` 1, which `disconnect` takes to tell them apart.
A link that does not exist is a no-op, not an error.
Use it to rewire a flow -- for example to insert a new block between two existing ones: disconnect a -> c, then connect a -> b and b -> c.
When several parallel links join the pair, name which one with *index* (0 is the first); leaving it out is then an error listing the candidates.
Branch order is what binds a DECIDE's `probs[n]` / `conditions[n]` to a target, so getting it wrong sends entities down the wrong path without any validation error.
*order* must list exactly the current targets of *source*, permuted.
Use `upsert_record` (section "resources") for a single change; this one is for setting several resources at once, or for deleting one by leaving it out.
A block's `resource_name` may name a resource or a resource set -- they share one namespace.
A calendar is optional: without one a model's clock is a plain number in the base time unit, which is the right choice for an abstract study.
Set one when the study is about real weeks -- weekday shifts, a holiday shutdown, a tariff or a campaign pinned to dates, or a client report that must say "Wednesday 10:00".
Once set, schedules may be authored as weekday grids, time series and orders may carry ISO timestamps, and results, charts, playback and exports all show wall-clock time.
Entity types name the things flowing through the model (CREATE's `e_type`) and carry the per-type WIP `holding_cost` used by the cost KPIs.
A model with no declared types still runs: everything is "DEFAULT".
ALWAYS set a run length for a model that cannot drain on its own -- one with an endless CREATE (max_arrivals 0), a failure, or a repeating capacity schedule.
Without it a run raises rather than hanging.
Without it a flow rate is re-evaluated only at events, which is exact for rates that change only then.
A rate that reads LEVEL(), FRACTION() or TNOW -- dL/dt = -k*L, logistic growth, an SIR model -- needs the grid: it is re-integrated every dt with Euler or RK4, the way Stella and Vensim do.
Static rates are untouched, and events inside a step stay exact.
Purely cosmetic -- it changes no behaviour and no KPI.
Call it once after building a model so a human opening it in the editor sees a readable diagram instead of a pile of blocks.
The same `$defs/<item>` the model-file schema uses (MCP resource naga://reference/schema), with the `$defs` it references.
Read it once before writing the first record of a section.
Record shape: schema $defs/<item>, see get_record_schema.
To change one field, list_records, edit, upsert.
An agent type's `python` cannot be written here: code needs the human's consent.
References to it elsewhere (TABLE("name"), a flow's "from", a block's resource_name, ...) come back as problems in the answer, so fix them in the same batch.
Two shapes: a 1-D table is `key,value` under a `key,value` header; a 2-D table is a header row of column keys whose first cell is EMPTY, then one row per key.
The file must be under the workspace root -- a path that escapes it is refused, and there is no argument that widens that.
A time series is a profile read by TS("name") -- a PV curve, a site load, a tariff by hour.
A level is a continuous quantity with bounds (battery energy, tank volume, stock on hand), read by LEVEL("name").
A flow moves quantity between levels at a rate that is an expression, read by FLOW("name").
Call this before writing any of those expressions.
Auxiliaries (AUX("name")) and delays (DELAY("name")) are the system-dynamics records that go with them.
Subscripts are the dimensions records run over.
Edit any of these with upsert_record / remove_record.
The file must be under the workspace root -- a path that escapes it is refused, and there is no argument that widens that.
Coordinates are layout coordinates -- metres once the model's background image declares a scale.
Travel time anywhere in the model is `distance / speed` along this graph, so this is what to read before reasoning about how long anything takes to move.
A node is a PLACE: a dock door, an aisle junction, a pick face.
Attach a block to it with the STATION `node` param and travel to and from that station becomes the shortest path along the segments.
Blocks whose `node` still names it come back as E_NETWORK_NODE_UNKNOWN problems.
Check `get_network`'s "unreachable" afterwards: a removal that strands a routing is an E_NETWORK_UNREACHABLE error.
The same number `DISTANCE("source", "target")` returns in an expression, so use it to sanity-check a travel time before writing one: a trip at speed v takes `distance / v`.
`distance` is null when no path joins them.
A sequence is the operation order a product follows through shared stations: a ROUTE block sends an entity whose `sequence` attribute names one to each step's STATION block in turn.
Call this before writing a CREATE `sequence` or an ASSIGN to entity.sequence, so the name and the stations are ones the model actually has.
An order is "make `quantity` of `entity_type` on routing `sequence`, released at `release`, due at `due`", both times in the model's BASE time unit.
A CREATE block in arrival mode "Orders" releases them; the run then reports per-order lateness and tardiness and a model-wide service level.
Columns: `id` (required), then any of release, due, quantity, entity_type, sequence, priority, source; every other column becomes a free attribute assigned onto the order's entities.
This is the shape an MES work-order export already has.
The file is read through the same root confinement as every other file tool: a path that escapes it is refused, and there is no argument that widens that.
An override path addresses the layout by name, not by index -- for example "resources.Server.capacity", "blocks.process_1.params.dist_params.rate" or "simulation.replications".
Scenarios are how you answer "A vs B, how sure are we"; run them with `run_scenarios`.
Validate first: a model with errors will not run.
Every KPI comes back as a mean with the half-width of its 95% confidence interval over replications; a half-width near the mean means you need more replications (see `run_to_precision`).
One replication gives no interval at all (null).
Use `resolve_data_bindings` first to preview what a binding would read.
The full frames stay in the workspace: page them out with `get_kpi_table`.
Use it when the digest is not enough -- to see per-resource detail, the per-entity log, or a time series.
Ask for the smallest window you need: `entity_log` and `timeseries` have thousands of rows.
A non-significant difference means "not distinguishable at this replication count", not "no difference".
A model without an `investment` section answers E_NO_INVESTMENT.
Use it instead of guessing a replication count: "how many runs do I need to call this number to within 5%".
If `met` comes back false, the cap or the time budget was hit first and the reported half-width is what you actually have.

Each check is one deterministic replication; a check with no violation passes.
Refused with E_LOOP_GRID without simulation.sd.
A steady-state model starts empty, which biases early observations low; the warm-up is the time to reset statistics at.
If `reliable` is false the run was too short to tell -- lengthen it rather than trusting the number.
Every factor is an override path plus a range, exactly like a scenario override but varying.
The budget is a HARD cap on replications, so start small (a few hundred) and raise it if `converged` is false.
Constraints are judged on confidence intervals, so a point may come back "unknown" rather than feasible or infeasible.
Give what the real system did (`targets`) and which parameters may move (`factors`, the same shape `optimize` takes).
The objective is the weighted sum of squared RELATIVE errors, so KPIs on different scales count equally.
A target with a `tolerance` gets a pass/fail verdict; read the per-target confidence interval too -- a pass whose interval is far wider than the tolerance has not really been demonstrated.
Starts from the model's data bindings and initial state, runs a terminating horizon with no warm-up, and answers "where is this heading".
The band is the empirical 5-95% range across replications -- where a single future run is likely to land -- NOT a confidence interval of the mean, which is the narrower `lb`/`ub` pair beside it.
An event's `kpi` may be any run KPI or a time-series peak, `timeseries/<series>/max`, which is how you ask "was the queue EVER above 8" rather than "was it on average".
Use `html` for the client-facing deliverable (it embeds the charts) and `json` when another program will read the numbers.
Runs `episodes` episodes of `nagasim.rl.SimEnv`, driving every pending decision at the named `policy` with `controller`.
Use this to compare "shortest" against "random" (or "roundrobin") before ever training anything, or to sanity-check a model's Policy-mode DECIDE wiring.
Every factor is swept per `design` and simulated `replications` times; the surrogate is then fit on the point means, weighted by their precision.
A binding is "this parameter comes from that column of that file", so this is how a model's numbers come from measurements instead of guesses.
Nothing here raises: a source that is missing, refused or unreadable comes back as a `problem` on its own row and simply is not applied.
Files must be under the workspace root, and a `sql`/`json_url` source is read only if the person who started this server allowed network access.
There is no argument that changes either: a refusal is final for you, and its `problem` tells the HUMAN what to re-run if they want it.
Call with `apply=true` to write the values into the model (undoable), or leave it false to preview.
`apply=true` still writes the whole value.
This is what makes a model a twin rather than a study.
A warm-started model needs no warm-up, and `run_model` defaults it to 0.
Pass no arguments to clear the initial state.
Give either a file path under the workspace root or an inline list of numbers.
The ranking is by AIC (lower is better) with KS/AD statistics alongside.
Apply the winner by setting the block's `distribution` and `dist_params` to the returned `spec`.
A plant mapping says what each key a plant sends asserts about the model (which block an item is in, how many units of a resource are busy, what a level holds).
The log's observations become the same trace events a run emits, so `blocks` and `resources` read exactly like a run's playback.
Both files are data under the workspace root.
This tool opens no connection and has no argument that could: watching a live plant is the person's own `naga plant watch` with their connections file.
`counts` says what was dropped, repaired or made up, by reason; `problems` carries the mapping's errors (then nothing is replayed) and the replay's warnings.
A twin is started by a person (`naga twin run`), reads their plant through their connections and writes a result every few seconds; this tool reads that result and nothing else.
`at` is model time, in `model.time_unit` from `model.epoch` (null where the source has no epoch).
`kpis` are end-of-horizon means with a confidence interval (`lb`, `ub`) and the 5-95% band of single replications; `points` are predictions at stated times.
`comparison` sets each prediction whose time has come beside the observed value: `inside` says whether it fell in the 5-95% band.
Readings overlap in time: this is evidence in distribution, not a test.
Read-only: this tool cannot deliver, approve, reject or address a recommendation, and no tool can.
The person who started the twin gave it candidate actions and one KPI (`kpi`, with `better`: "higher" or "lower").
After each forecast the twin runs every candidate from the same plant state on the same random numbers (`crn`) and sets it beside doing nothing.

Only "better" items have a `rank`, an `id` and a `status`: "proposed" (shown, not delivered), "delivered" (written to the person's own outbox, unanswered), "taken", "rejected", "expired" or "dropped".
With `status` "none", say `reason`: "no_forecast" (a source is down or the state was refused: see `get_twin_forecast`), "none_better", "kpi", "replications" or "failed".
`standing` lists the actions a person took, which every later forecast now assumes until a person ends one (`ended` lists those).
This is what the model says, in distribution: not a causal claim about the plant, and one effect outside its band proves little.
A proposal is acted on by a person, in their own queue or in the editor; if asked to approve or send one, say that you cannot.
Use this FIRST when you are about to build a model and do not yet know the vocabulary.
The `type` strings it returns are exactly what `add_block` expects.
Plugin block types appear here automatically.
`multi_output` marks the only types allowed more than one outgoing link (DECIDE, LOGIC): every other block may have at most one.
Use this before `add_block`/`update_block` whenever you are unsure which params a type takes -- passing an unknown key is an error, and the defaults tell you what you may safely leave out.
Each description is its first sentence unless `detail` is true.
Pass `block_type` (CREATE, DELAY, PROCESS, ...) to get only the ones that block is usually given; omit it for everything, including plugin entries.
The names are what goes in a block's `distribution` param, a link delay, or a failure's uptime/downtime.
Call describe_distribution for parameter meanings.
Use it when choosing between, say, Exponential and Lognormal for a service time, or when you need the exact parameter names for `dist_params`.
Every numeric parameter also accepts an expression string, so a rate may depend on an entity attribute.
Read this before writing any expression: it is a restricted-Python subset (an AST allow-list, never eval), so anything not listed here is refused at validation time rather than at run time.
Call this after each batch of edits and ALWAYS before running.
Errors stop a run; warnings (code prefix W_) do not, but usually point at a modelling mistake.
`requires_run_length` tells you whether the model can drain on its own -- if it is true and the run length is 0, a run will be refused.
With `blocks` or `sections`: those in full, each field with its meaning.
Generated from the registries and the JSON Schema (resource naga://reference/schema), so it is never out of date.
The fast way to build a model: call get_model_format once, write the file, fix what the answer lists with one more write_model, then run_model and save_model.
The layout is read and validated exactly as a model file on disk is; it replaces an open model of the same name as one undo step.
Blocks given no position are laid out automatically.
Use it to explain behaviour, such as why a queue grows or where entities get stuck.
The run is kept between calls, one per model, so the usual loop is: set stops and watches, call again and again, and read `debug_inspect` whenever it returns.
A stop fires on a change -- an entity entering a block, an expression going from false to true -- so calling again always moves on.
Nothing here changes the results: a run that is stopped, stepped and inspected ends with the same numbers as `run_model` with one replication and the same seed.
`back` undoes the previous call's move: the run is rebuilt where that call found it, by replaying the same seed and decisions, so nothing is approximated.
`hits` lists every stop that fired during the call and is read at every return, so it can be non-empty beside any state, not only "stop".
Then a start or `restart` happens (with the new stops and watches, if given), then `decisions` are applied, then on a continuing run the new stops and watches take effect, then the run moves.
A refused decision answers with an error before the run moves: a continuing run keeps its stops and watches as they were, but the decisions listed before the refused one stay applied.
A start or `restart` is not undone by a later error in the same call.
Call it after `debug_run` returns.
With no argument it is the overview: how many entities sit in each block, every resource's state, every level's value and the decisions waiting.
`block` adds that block's queue and entities; `entity` adds one live entity's attributes, the model's own included.
Counts are per block of the top level: a block inside a submodel instance is counted with its instance, and `block` then answers for the instance (see the "name" it returns).
Use it for a decision question ("how many cranes do we need?"), then follow the next_step in every answer.
The study keeps its state in the folder; pass the returned `study` to the other study tools.
Send the plan card in the same call with `changes` (the same keys and shapes as study_update).
Call it first on an existing study folder.
A list key replaces the whole list.
Nothing here can mark the study accepted.
Always send the complete model file and a one-line note.
A model that does not validate or run is stored as a draft with its problems, not refused: read "problems", fix the model, step again.
With no goal KPI the count is 10 and provisional.
A cap reached makes the "precision" check partial, never failed.
`changes` (the same keys and shapes as study_update) is recorded first, in the same call, so a step that also records the goals or a validation needs one call, not two.
Both are listed in "normalised".
When the waits cannot be rebuilt the goal stays not_verified and "tail_note" says why.
A version has no report file by default (the answer is the light output); study_report writes it on request.
Any other model answers E_STUDY_NOT_APPLICABLE with the reason, so the person is asked for another validation.
Call it only with the person's own words, after they have explicitly accepted; never on your own judgment.
It changes the label, not the checks: open issues stay listed.
Use it when a later step made things worse.
Steps do not write it, to keep the default output light.
It reruns the version's stored model with the step's stored replications and seed, so the numbers match the step.
Use it when the person is satisfied with the study.
Use it to check the model looks like the process.
Without matplotlib a png request answers with the text and a "note".
In chats that support MCP Apps the page appears inline, with buttons to revert to a version or accept the study; elsewhere this is a short summary and the path of the page file.
It exists for the in-chat page, which fetches it itself so the HTML never enters the conversation; assistants should call study_show instead.
Rate parameters are varied as rates (a higher rate is a shorter time).
Without `apply`, lists the ones that validate, run and pass the law checks on the last version, with their effect on the goal KPIs in one short run (indicative only).
With `apply`, answers the model layout with that module added: review it, then send it to study_step; this tool never steps the study.
On request only; it needs nagasim[plot] (matplotlib).
`discussion` is your own interpretation, placed in section 8.
writeup.md carries the study's own text as written (Markdown, not escaped for HTML), so treat it as text to read, not to embed in a page.
Scroll on screen; print to PDF gives one slide per page.
Use it when no tool in your list is obviously right.
